ayasofya: The great church built by Justinian in 537, for almost a thousand years the largest in the Christian world, then a mosque and a museum and now a mosque again. The 55-metre dome seems to float above the hall, and from the upper gallery you see the Byzantine mosaics up close.
sultanahmet: The Sultan Ahmed Mosque, called the Blue Mosque for the blue tiles inside, has six minarets and a cascade of domes. In front is the ancient Hippodrome of Constantinople, with the Egyptian obelisk, the Serpent Column and the German Fountain.
topkapi: The residence of the Ottoman sultans for about four hundred years, on a promontory over the Bosphorus and the Golden Horn. Four courtyards, the imperial kitchens, the Treasury with the Spoonmaker's Diamond, the sacred relics and the Harem, the private quarters of the sultan's family.
cisterna: A huge 6th-century underground reservoir, with 336 columns holding up the vaults in soft light. At the far end are the two Medusa heads used as column bases, one upside down and one on its side.
archeo: Three museums in one complex at the foot of Topkapı: the Archaeology Museum with the Sidon sarcophagi (including the Alexander Sarcophagus), the Museum of the Ancient Orient and the Tiled Kiosk. You walk there through Gülhane Park.
bazar: One of the world's oldest covered markets, founded in 1461: over 60 covered streets and about 4,000 shops selling carpets, ceramics, lamps, jewellery and leather. You wander a maze of painted vaults, with little courtyards and cafés.
suleymaniye: The great mosque of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, built in the 16th century by the architect Sinan on one of Istanbul's hills. The interior is sober and bright, with a 53-metre dome, and from the garden you see the whole Golden Horn.
spezie: The 17th-century covered market next to Galata Bridge: stalls of spices, tea, dried fruit, lokum (Turkish delight) and cheese. Outside, on the Eminönü quay, are the ferries, the fried-fish boats and the crowds crossing the bridge.
galata: The 67-metre stone tower from 1348, built by the Genoese of Galata: from the top you see the whole Golden Horn, the Old City and the Bosphorus. Around it are the steep streets of Karaköy, with cafés, design shops and the Tünel funicular.
istiklal: Beyoğlu's long pedestrian avenue, run by a red vintage tram: shops, bookshops, galleries, covered passages such as Çiçek Pasajı, churches and 19th-century buildings. It ends at Taksim Square, the great crossroads of the modern city.
bosforo: Crossing the Bosphorus by ferry is the cheapest way to see Istanbul from the water: from the Eminönü piers, ferries leave for Üsküdar and Kadıköy on the Asian side, with the Old City and the Süleymaniye Mosque behind you. On deck you can buy tea served in little glass cups.
kadikoy: The liveliest district on the Asian side: a market with stalls of fish, olives, cheese and sweets, the Bull statue and streets of cafés, bookshops and bars. A little further south, Moda is a residential area with parks and a seafront on the Sea of Marmara.
